chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Hammad ibn Isa, from Rib'i, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them), who said:
"There is no harm if a poor person performs Hajj on behalf of another poor person."

As for what Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa from Ibrahim ibn Uqba, who said: I wrote to him asking him about a man who performed Hajj on behalf of a poor person who had never performed Hajj before. Does that one Hajj suffice for both of them as the Hajj of Islam, or not? Make it clear to me, O my master, if God wills. He (peace be upon him) wrote: "That does not suffice."
This is understood to mean when the poor person has wealth, because if the matter is as we mentioned, that does not suffice for him.
And we have narrated it in the report of Sa'd ibn Abi Khalaf from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him).
It is also possible that his saying (peace be upon him) "That does not suffice" means for the one who performs Hajj, if he becomes poor.
Because whoever performs Hajj on behalf of another and then becomes poor, Hajj becomes obligatory upon him.
This is indicated by what has been narrated.

key_terms.صَّرُورَة: A poor person who cannot afford Hajj

ai.seo_question: Does one Hajj suffice for both the poor person and the one performing Hajj on their behalf?
ai.summary: This passage from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* explores the juristic nuance of Hajj performed on behalf of a *sarrurah* (a poor person lacking sufficient funds), reconciling apparent contradictions by distinguishing between the financial status of the proxy and the principal. It highlights the Shia scholarly method of contextualizing hadith, suggesting that the restriction applies specifically when the proxy becomes impoverished or if the principal possesses wealth, thereby ensuring the validity of the obligatory Hajj. This reflects the broader principle that Hajj is an obligation of ability, and its delegation requires careful consideration of economic capacity.
